# BM25 scoring

BM25 ranks a document for a query by summing, over the query's terms, a weight per
term that grows with how often the term appears in the document and with how rare
the term is across the collection. The two forces it balances are term frequency
saturation and document length normalisation.

The score for a document d and query terms q is the sum over each term t in q of:

    IDF(t) * ( f(t,d) * (k1 + 1) ) / ( f(t,d) + k1 * (1 - b + b * |d| / avgdl) )

f(t,d) is how many times t occurs in d, |d| is the length of d in tokens, avgdl is
the mean document length in the collection, and k1 and b are the two parameters.

The inverse document frequency term is usually the smoothed form:

    IDF(t) = ln( 1 + (N - n(t) + 0.5) / (n(t) + 0.5) )

d b are the two parameters.

The inverse document frequency term is usually the smoothed form:

    IDF(t) = ln( 1 + (N - n(t) + 0.5) / (n(t) + 0.5) )

where N is the number of documents and n(t) is the number of documents containing
t. The additive 1 inside the logarithm keeps the value non-negative even when a
term appears in more than half the collection, which the unsmoothed classic form
does not.

BM25 is a bag-of-words model. It ignores word order entirely, which is why it
cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog". That is a real limitation and
the reason phrase queries need support beyond the scoring function.

# Building an evaluation dataset honestly

The dataset is the most important artefact in a retrieval evaluation and the easiest
one to get quietly wrong. A dataset that flatters the system produces a number that
looks impressive and cannot survive a question.

## Choose the relevant passage by topic, not by retrieval output

The tempting shortcut is to run the retriever, take its top result, and record that
as the relevant passage. The resulting metric measures agreement with itself and will
be near perfect. It is circular, and it is the most common way an evaluation number
becomes meaningless.

Decide what is relevant by reading the corpus. The judgement must be independent of
the system being measured, or the measurement is worthless.

## Never score a broken case as a miss

g the corpus. The judgement must be independent of
the system being measured, or the measurement is worthless.

## Never score a broken case as a miss

If a dataset case cites a passage that the index cannot resolve, the dataset and the
corpus have diverged. Scoring that case zero silently converts a broken input into a
worse metric, and the number that comes out looks valid.

The correct behaviour is to fail the run. A dataset error and a retrieval failure are
different things and must not be averaged together.

## Detect staleness, do not hide it

to fail the run. A dataset error and a retrieval failure are
different things and must not be averaged together.

## Detect staleness, do not hide it

If the corpus is edited, character offsets move and a handle that once pointed at the
right passage may now point at different text. A case like that is stale. It should be
reported and excluded, never scored as a miss, because the miss would be an artefact
of editing rather than a property of retrieval.

## How many cases

Twenty-five is a floor for publishing a number, and even then it is underpowered. A
difference of a few points between two systems on twenty-five cases is noise. Report
the case count with every metric, and treat small differences as unresolved rather
than as improvements.

# Chunking

Retrieval does not return documents; it returns passages. If passages are cut badly,
no scoring function can recover the relevance that the cut destroyed.

## Why chunk at all

A whole document is usually too much context and too diffuse a signal. A document
about six topics will match almost any query weakly, and the matched text will be
buried in material that has nothing to do with the question. Splitting into passages
makes each unit about fewer things, so the match is sharper and the reader gets
sent to the relevant part rather than to the top of a long file.

## Fixed size against paragraph boundaries

Cutting every N characters produces uniform chunks and is trivial to implement, but
it slices mid-sentence and can separate a heading from the text it introduces.

y N characters produces uniform chunks and is trivial to implement, but
it slices mid-sentence and can separate a heading from the text it introduces.

Cutting on paragraph boundaries respects the author's own structure. The cost is
varying chunk sizes, which is exactly what BM25's length normalisation exists to
handle. This project accumulates paragraphs until a character target is reached and
only hard-splits a single paragraph when it is larger than the target on its own.

## Overlap

If a fact spans a boundary, a chunk that ends mid-fact answers nothing and a chunk
that begins mid-fact is confusing. Overlap repeats the tail of one chunk at the
start of the next, so the fact appears whole in at least one of them.

that begins mid-fact is confusing. Overlap repeats the tail of one chunk at the
start of the next, so the fact appears whole in at least one of them.

The cost is duplicated text: the index grows, and a query can return the same
passage twice under two handles. Overlap is worth it when questions span boundaries
often, and wasted when the documents are already written in short independent
sections.

## The measurement that matters

Chunk size and overlap are hyperparameters, and the honest way to choose them is to
build the index twice and run the same evaluation against both. The difference in
recall is the answer. Anything else is a preference dressed up as a decision.

# Inverted indexes

An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents that contain it. That
inversion is what makes search fast: instead of reading every document to see
whether it mentions a term, you look the term up and get the documents directly.

The structure is a dictionary from term to a posting list. Each posting records
which document the term occurs in, and usually how many times, because BM25 needs
the term frequency. Postings are normally kept in document order so that two posting
lists can be intersected efficiently when a query has several terms.

## Why the dictionary is the expensive part

## Why the dictionary is the expensive part

The posting lists are large but predictable. The dictionary is the part that decides
how the index is stored: a real search engine keeps a sorted term dictionary with a
prefix-compressed structure so that a term lookup is a binary search over compressed
blocks. This project uses a plain dictionary because the corpus fits in memory, and
the tradeoff is stated rather than hidden.

## Segmented indexes

Production engines such as Lucene do not rewrite one giant index on every update.
They write a new immutable segment and search all segments together, merging them in
the background. Immutability makes concurrent reads safe without locking, and
merging keeps the number of segments bounded.

Building one flat index is enough at this scale. The reason segments exist is worth
knowing, because it explains why a search engine can accept writes continuously while
this design must rebuild from scratch.

# Lexical against semantic retrieval

Lexical retrieval matches the words actually present in the text. Semantic retrieval
matches meaning, by comparing learned vector representations of the query and the
passages. They fail in different places, and knowing which failure you have is worth
more than picking a side.

## Where lexical wins

Exact identifiers. A model number, an error code, a product SKU, a function name, a
person's surname. Semantic models routinely miss these because a rare token has almost
no representation to generalise from, while BM25 scores them highly precisely because
they are rare. Technical documentation, code, and support tickets are full of such
tokens.

alise from, while BM25 scores them highly precisely because
they are rare. Technical documentation, code, and support tickets are full of such
tokens.

Lexical retrieval is also explainable by construction: a result can be justified term
by term, and a miss can be shown to be an absent term rather than a lost meaning.

## Where semantic wins

Paraphrase and vocabulary mismatch. A question about "make the site faster" and a
passage about "reducing page load latency" share no tokens and are trivially related
by meaning. BM25 scores that pair at zero and cannot be tuned into finding it.

## Why measure before combining

## Why measure before combining

Hybrid retrieval that merges both rankings is the usual answer and is often genuinely
better. It is also more code, more dependencies, and a second thing that can fail. The
only defensible reason to add it is a measured baseline showing which errors lexical
retrieval makes, and evidence that the semantic component fixes that class of error
rather than merely adding a different set of misses.

Build the lexical baseline first. Its failures name the problem the next component
has to solve.

# Mean reciprocal rank

Mean reciprocal rank, abbreviated MRR, measures where the first relevant result
appears in the ranking. For each query you take the reciprocal of the rank of the
first relevant passage: 1 if it is first, one half if it is second, one third if it
is third. Queries that find nothing contribute zero. MRR is the mean of those values
across all queries.

## What it captures that recall does not

Recall@K does not care about order within the top K. A relevant passage at rank one
and the same passage at rank ten score identically at K=10. MRR does care, and it
answers a different question: when the system does find the right thing, does it put
it near the top?

answers a different question: when the system does find the right thing, does it put
it near the top?

That matters whenever a human or a model reads only the first result. If the right
passage is reliably found but usually sits at rank seven, recall looks respectable
and the product is still bad.

## The limitation to state out loud

MRR ignores every relevant passage after the first. A query with five relevant
passages where one is found at rank two scores the same as a query with a single
relevant passage found at rank two. It is a single-number summary, and like every
single-number summary it hides structure.

single-number summary it hides structure.

Report MRR next to Recall@K rather than instead of it. MRR tells you about ranking
quality among the successes; recall tells you how often there is a success at all.
A run where recall is high and MRR is low is a reordering problem, which is a much
cheaper fix than a retrieval problem.

# Recall, precision, and which one to report

Recall asks what fraction of the relevant passages were found. Precision asks what
fraction of the returned passages were relevant. They trade against each other, and
which one matters depends entirely on what happens next.

For a retrieval step that feeds a language model, recall is usually the constraint
that binds. If the passage containing the answer is not in the retrieved set, no
amount of good generation will produce a correct answer grounded in a source. Extra
passages cost tokens and can distract, but a missing passage makes the task
impossible. That is why this project reports Recall@K and MRR and treats precision as
a secondary signal.

## Recall@K

a secondary signal.

## Recall@K

Recall@K is the fraction of the relevant passages that appear in the top K results.
It is reported at several K because the answer to "is it good" depends on how much
context the next stage can afford. Recall@1 measures whether the single best passage
is right, which matters when only one passage will be shown. Recall@10 tolerates a
noisier ranking that a later stage will filter.

Reporting a single K hides this. A system can look strong at K=10 and be useless at
K=1, and only the table of several cut-offs reveals it.

## Why not precision alone

e K hides this. A system can look strong at K=10 and be useless at
K=1, and only the table of several cut-offs reveals it.

## Why not precision alone

A retriever that returns every passage in the corpus has perfect recall and useless
precision. A retriever that returns one passage has perfect precision when it is
right and zero recall when the corpus needs two sources to answer. Neither number is
meaningful by itself, which is why evaluation should always report at least one
recall-oriented metric and the failure cases that produced it.

# Term saturation and length normalisation

The two parameters in BM25 are not tuning knobs to be optimised blindly. Each has
a meaning, and knowing it is the difference between adjusting them from evidence
and adjusting them until a number looks better.

## Term saturation, k1

The term frequency factor is f(t,d) * (k1 + 1) / (f(t,d) + k1 * ...). As f(t,d)
grows, the numerator and the denominator grow together, so the factor approaches
an asymptote instead of growing without bound. That asymptote is the point: a
document containing a term ten times is more relevant than one containing it once,
but not ten times more relevant. The tenth occurrence carries almost no new
information.

term ten times is more relevant than one containing it once,
but not ten times more relevant. The tenth occurrence carries almost no new
information.

k1 sets how quickly the curve flattens. At k1 equal to zero the formula degenerates
to pure binary presence and term frequency is ignored entirely. As k1 grows the
factor approaches linear in f(t,d). Values between 1.2 and 2.0 are the common
range; 1.2 is the default in this project.

## Length normalisation, b

Long documents contain more of every term by accident, simply because they are
long. The |d| / avgdl ratio corrects for that, scaled by b.

isation, b

Long documents contain more of every term by accident, simply because they are
long. The |d| / avgdl ratio corrects for that, scaled by b.

At b equal to zero there is no normalisation at all and long documents are
systematically favoured, because they have more chances to match. At b equal to one
normalisation is full. The usual value is 0.75, which accepts that a genuinely long
document probably does discuss more topics and should not be penalised completely.

b matters more than k1 in practice. A corpus of wildly uneven document lengths with
b set too low will be dominated by its longest documents, and the fix is a single
parameter rather than a rewrite.

# Tokenisation

Tokenisation decides what counts as a word, and every later stage inherits that
decision. Indexing and querying must tokenise identically, or a term will be written
into the index under one form and looked up under another, and the retrieval failure
will appear as a scoring mystery.

The baseline used here: lowercase the text, split on any character that is not a
letter or a digit, and drop single-character tokens. Lowercasing makes matching
case-insensitive, which is almost always wanted. Splitting on punctuation separates
trailing commas and brackets from the words they touch. Dropping one-character tokens
removes noise at negligible cost.

## Stemming

Stemming reduces words to a common root so that "index", "indexing" and "indexed" all
match the same term. It improves recall on morphological variants and it makes the
system harder to reason about.

The specific cost is diagnosability. With stemming, a miss has two possible causes:
the term is genuinely absent, or the stemmer mapped it somewhere unexpected. Without
stemming there is one cause and it is checkable by searching the file.

## Stopwords

Removing common words such as "the" and "of" shrinks the index and speeds scoring,
because those terms carry little discriminating information and appear in nearly every
passage. The cost is that a query which is mostly stopwords loses most of its terms
and can return nonsense or nothing. Phrases and titles are full of such queries.

Both choices are legitimate. The point is that they are choices with costs, they
change the meaning of a metric, and they belong in a written decision rather than in
an unexamined line of code.

# Tracing a retrieval run

A retrieval system that returns an answer without recording how it got there is not
debuggable. When a query returns the wrong passage, the useful question is not "what
did it return" but "what did it consider, what did it score them, and what did it
discard".

## What a trace should record

did it return" but "what did it consider, what did it score them, and what did it
discard".

## What a trace should record

The tokenised query, so that a surprising result can be traced to tokenisation rather
than to scoring. For each term, how many passages matched it, because a term matching
zero passages explains an empty result immediately and a term matching every passage
explains a useless one. The scored candidates before truncation to k, because the
passage that was wanted is very often at rank six when five were returned. And
timings, because a ranking that is correct but slow is a different problem from one
that is fast and wrong.

## Why the discarded candidates matter

that is fast and wrong.

## Why the discarded candidates matter

Reporting only the top k hides the near misses. A system returning five results where
the relevant passage is at rank six looks broken; the same system returning ten
results looks fine. Without the pre-truncation ranking you cannot tell the difference
between "the passage was not found" and "the passage was found but cut off", and
those have completely different fixes.

## The cost

Recording a trace means keeping intermediate state that is otherwise thrown away. In
a high-throughput system that is real overhead. The tradeoff to make deliberately: log
traces always in development and on a sampled fraction in production, rather than
never or always.

# Why the index is a readable file

Storing a search index as a plain readable file rather than a compact binary is a
deliberate trade, and the trade is worth naming.

## What it buys

A reviewer can open the index and check it. The parameters are at the top, the posting
lists are visible, and the arithmetic in the scoring formula can be verified by hand
against the stored counts. That matters enormously when the index is the artefact a
reader has to trust: a number produced by an opaque file can only be believed, while a
number produced by a readable one can be checked.

reader has to trust: a number produced by an opaque file can only be believed, while a
number produced by a readable one can be checked.

It also diffs. When the chunking changes, the index diff shows exactly which passages
appeared, moved or disappeared, which is how a change in recall gets explained instead
of guessed at. A binary format would show a changed file and nothing more.

## What it costs

Size and speed. JSON is larger than a compact binary encoding and slower to parse, and
holding the whole structure in memory bounds the corpus by available RAM. The
alternative for a large corpus is a real index format, and adopting one would import a
dependency and hide the arithmetic this project exists to show.

## The honest framing

This is the right trade at the documented scale, for a tool whose purpose is
explainability. It is the wrong trade for a search engine serving millions of
documents, and saying so is part of the decision rather than a weakness in it.
